/-!
# Digit $2$ in base $3$ representation of $2^n$

*References:*
- [Some Unconventional Problems in Number Theory](https://doi.org/10.2307/2689842)
  by *Paul Erdös*, Mathematics Magazine 52, no. 2, p. 67, 1979
- [arxiv/2107.12475](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12475)
  **Hardness of busy beaver value BB(15)** by *Tristan Stérin, Damien Woods*
- [Hardness of Busy Beaver Value BB(15)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72621-7_9)
  by *Tristan Stérin, Damien Woods*, Reachability Problems, Lecture Notes in Computer Science
  15050, Springer, Cham (2024)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Arxiv.«2107.12475»

/--
For $n > 8$, $2^n$ is not the the sum of distinct powers of $3$. Expressed here in terms of the base $3$ digits of $n$.

This conjecture is equivalent to the halting of a $15$-state $2$-symbol Turing Machine.

TODO(lezeau): Formalize the Turing Machine version of this problem.

Source: *Hardness of Busy Beaver Value BB(15)*: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-72621-7_9
This is also https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12475.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem CollatzLike (n : ℕ) (hn : 8 < n) : 2 ∈ Nat.digits 3 (2^n) := by
  sorry

/--
For $n = 8$, $2$ is not contained in the base $3$ digits of $n$.
-/
@[category test, AMS 5 11]
theorem two_not_in_digits_three_pow_eight : 2 ∉ Nat.digits 3 (2^8) := by norm_num

end Arxiv.«2107.12475»

findings.description: The docstring at line 40 says the conjecture is equivalent to the halting of a 15-state, 2-symbol Turing machine. For the machine constructed in the cited paper, the polarity is reversed: halting is equivalent to the conjecture being false. The number-theoretic Lean statement itself is correct.
findings.source_evidence: Stérin–Woods, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12475, abstract and §1.1, Theorem 1: the explicit 15-state, 2-symbol machine “halts if and only if Erdős' conjecture is false.” The Springer chapter abstract, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72621-7_9, says the same.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the sentence to say that the conjecture is equivalent to the non-halting, on blank input, of the paper's explicit 15-state, 2-symbol Turing machine.

findings.description: The final phrase of line 38 says the formulation uses the base-3 digits of n, but the Lean correctly uses the digits of 2^n. These are different conditions: for example, 9 = 100₃ has no digit 2, whereas 2^9 = 200222₃ does.
findings.source_evidence: Stérin–Woods, arXiv:2107.12475v2, §1.1, Conjecture 1: “For all natural numbers n > 8 there is at least one digit 2 in the base 3 representation of 2^n.” https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12475
findings.suggested_fix: Replace “the base $3$ digits of $n$” with “the base $3$ digits of $2^n$”. Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

findings.description: The docstring at line 52 says that 2 is absent from the ternary digits of n = 8. This is false, since 8 = 22₃. The Lean theorem correctly concerns 2^8 = 256 = 100111₃. Both digit expansions and the theorem's assertion were checked in Lean.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős, Some Unconventional Problems in Number Theory, Mathematics Magazine 52(2) (1979), p. 67, explicitly gives “2^8 = 256 = 3^5 + 3^2 + 3 + 1”: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-22.pdf. Stérin–Woods §1.2 likewise lists 256's ternary representation as 100111.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to “The base $3$ representation of $2^8$ contains no digit $2$.” Leave the proved theorem unchanged.

reformulations.difference: Erdős's original statement excludes representations of 2^n as sums of distinct powers of 3; Lean instead asserts that its ternary digit list contains 2. The Stérin–Woods paper explicitly presents both formulations.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every ternary digit is 0, 1, or 2. Absence of 2 means all coefficients in the unique base-3 expansion are 0 or 1, so the number is precisely the sum of the distinct powers corresponding to its 1-digits. Conversely, a sum of distinct powers of 3 has coefficients 0 or 1 and requires no carrying, so it contains no ternary digit 2. Negating this equivalence gives the Lean condition. Little-endian ordering in Nat.digits does not affect membership.

sources_consulted: Paul Erdős, Some Unconventional Problems in Number Theory, Mathematics Magazine 52(2) (1979), p. 67; https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-22.pdf (accessible copy of the cited DOI https://doi.org/10.2307/2689842).

https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/ and https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html — archive and bibliographic identification of the original paper.

review.notes: No substantive mathematical misformalization was found in either theorem; all findings concern documentation only. The research-open tag agrees with the consulted sources. Scratch checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiled successfully, verified the n = 8 and n = 9 cases, proved the classification of excluded exponents through 8, and computationally found only exponents 0, 2, and 8 without a ternary digit 2 through n = 1000. The test theorem has no sorry dependency. The distinct-power-sum equivalence is justified above; only its digit-restriction component, not the full sum equivalence, was proved in scratch Lean.
